source.title: Analyzing Fine-Tuning Representation Shift for Multimodal LLMs Steering
source.authors: Pegah Khayatan; Mustafa Shukor; Jayneel Parekh; Arnaud Dapogny; Matthieu Cord

record.tranche_reason: The study adds a contrast-derived activation vector and measures harmful-prompt safety and responses to benign prevention prompts. This is a conceptual test of directional steering for refusal, but it does not apply the original harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream direction or its all-layer, all-position ablation.
record.gate_note: The safety application derives its own vector from unsafe responses to harmful content presented with an image and safe responses to the same content presented as text, then adds it at one layer. The paper also reports baseline safety rates by modality; those do not test the single-direction claim. Other steering experiments concern answer types, caption styles, or gender debiasing and are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper adds a difference-in-means activation vector (safe text-only responses minus unsafe image-present responses) at layer 19 of Qwen2-VL-Instruct. It reports the refusal-based ASR before and after, plus refusal on benign prevention queries. That is an additive-steering test of a single refusal-related direction in a new setting (an MLLM), using a different contrast from the original harmful-minus-harmless one. It has no ablation arm.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors present the safety-guard vector as one application of their training-free steering framework: it raises refusal of harmful requests in Qwen2-VL-Instruct while keeping helpful answers to prevention queries. They cite Arditi et al. only as related work on steering refusals.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an activation-difference steering vector, but derives it from safe text-only and unsafe image-present versions of harmful content, then adds it at layer 19 with α = 1. It does not use the original direction or test ablation.
record.method_sensitivity: The safety result is reported only for layer 19 and α = 1; no safety-specific sweep over layer or strength is reported.

fits_no_version.finding: For LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2-VL-Instruct and Idefics2, harmful prompts with a malicious image yield more non-refused responses than the same content with a blank image. The gap is strongest for Qwen2-VL (358 vs 105 of 733).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MLLM safety refusal is weaker when harmful content is conveyed through an image than through text.

record.problems: The safety steering evaluation is limited to Qwen2-VL-Instruct and a portion of MM-SafetyBench. Refusal and safety are assessed by string matching, which the paper notes can misclassify useful responses containing matched strings. No uncertainty estimates or null-direction control are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported safety-steering results were omitted.

untested.parts: Directional ablation removing refusal; adding the vector inducing refusal on clearly harmless requests; the original harmful-minus-harmless direction; all-layer/all-position intervention; general capability benchmarks; models other than Qwen2-VL-Instruct.
Image-based attacks are not analysed as suppressing a refusal direction, and there is no adversarial training.
Single versus multiple directions not compared.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer. Text-vs-image modality is used to build the vector, but transfer of a direction is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: Evidence is thin: one model, 100 prompts, string-match ASR, a single layer and α, and no random-vector control or uncertainty. The vector contrasts refused against complied responses to equivalent harmful content across modalities. It is therefore closer to a refusal/compliance direction than V1's harmful-minus-harmless direction. T3 (new setting: MLLM) would also be defensible.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate the direction; does not test whether adding the original harmful-minus-harmless direction makes the model refuse harmless requests; does not test all layers and positions; checks usefulness only on prevention queries, not general capability.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.
Does not test attacks suppressing the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
Does not compare a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
Does not separate harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Does not test transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
Does not vary refusal training or test when a removable direction emerges.

rows.subject: Qwen2-VL-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Added a safety-guard steering vector to activations at layer 19, with α = 1.
rows.note: The vector is derived from safe text-only versus unsafe image-present samples, not the original harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction.
rows.check: State is correct. The vector is a refusal-vs-compliance contrast, not harmful-minus-harmless. The paper does not say whether the 100 evaluation prompts are disjoint from the Table 8 samples used to build the vector.

rows.subject: Qwen2-VL-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Added the safety-guard steering vector at layer 19, with α = 1.

conditions.value: helpful (not refusal) response count, reported as 1 − ASR

rows.note: The authors say manual inspection found the three responses counted as non-helpful did provide useful instructions, but contained strings matched by the refusal-string metric.
rows.check: Read as a capability/utility-retention check, not a weakened refusal effect. Helpful responses went 100→97/100, and the authors say manual inspection showed the 3 flagged responses were in fact helpful (string-match false positives). So utility is kept nearly in full; 'partial' misstates it.

rows.note: Reported as an ASR-related unsafe-response count; this baseline modality comparison does not test the refusal direction.

relationships.condition: Qwen2-VL-Instruct, additive steering at layer 19 with α=1 on harmful MM-SafetyBench image+typography prompts, string-match refusal metric
relationships.reason: Adding one contrast-derived vector cut non-refusal from 45/100 to 5/100 (r1), while prevention-query helpfulness stayed ~100/100 (r2). This is consistent with a single additive direction inducing refusal; it comes from one model, n=100, with no control vector.
relationships.display_finding: Vector addition reduced non-refusal from 45/100 to 5/100 while prevention-query helpfulness remained about 100/100.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Qwen2-VL-Instruct safety steering on the reported harmful-prompt evaluation, with a benign prevention-query check
reader_labels.reason: Adding the study's safety vector reduced reported ASR from 45/100 to 5/100, while helpful prevention responses changed from 100/100 to 97/100 (r1–r2); this supports only the tested steering effect, not the original direction or its broader claims.
